## Abstract

Attitudes are argued to reflect widespread cultural information – information that can be revealed

through language from contemporary and historical time. Yet research directly quantifying the

relationship between attitudes and language patterns at-scale remains limited. Here, we address the

question of whether and how attitudes are related to language by combining data from implicit and

explicit attitudes of >200,000 participants towards 55 topics alongside language representations from

word embeddings trained on 9 contemporary text corpora and 200 years of historical books. Results

show strong relationships between implicit attitudes and language patterns, persisting beyond explicit

attitudes, cultural attitudes, and even across two centuries. Explicit attitudes were not related to language

in any corpus or time-period. Theoretically, language and implicit attitudes reflect widespread and

historically-persistent statistical regularities, while explicit attitudes are filtered through values/goals. And

methodologically, results provide validation of emerging research using language to expand the study of

implicit social cognition.

## Introduction

Attitudes – evaluations of a target person, object, group, or concept on a positive/negative dimension –

are ubiquitous in society (Albarracin & Shavitt, 2018; Eagly & Chaiken, 1998), and indispensable for understanding human cognition and behavior (Allport, 1935). While debates remain around the

measurement of attitudes and their relations to behavior (Gawronski, 2019; Jost, 2019; Kurdi et al., 2021; Schimmack, 2019; Vianello & Bar-Anan, 2021), most perspectives agree that attitudes are shaped by

widespread cultural information (Payne et al., 2017). In other words, most theories of attitudes assume that cultural information (or collective representations and statistics that associate some concepts with goodness and other concepts with badness; (Durkheim, 1924; Moscovici, 1994) is so pervasive that it will

necessarily come to be internalized and reflected in attitudes as well (e.g., Banaji, 2001; Fiske et al., 1998). Recent perspectives, such as Payne and colleagues’ bias of crowds model (2017) argue that cultural

patterns may be especially reflected in implicit attitudes – more automatic attitudes measured using indirect techniques – whereas explicit, self-reported and consciously-controllable attitudes are more likely

to be filtered through personal values. While this assumed relationship between culture and attitudes is long-standing in the field, there remain, to our knowledge, no direct, quantitative examinations that

demonstrate whether, and to what extent, attitudes are related to the widespread, information embedded in real-world environments measured at-scale.

Of course, part of the difficulty in addressing this research question arises from the difficulty in

systematically quantifying this diffuse idea of “cultural information.” In the current manuscript, we rely on the tools of natural language processing (NLP) techniques, specifically word embeddings, applied to

massive corpora of billions of words of naturalistic text, to quantify cultural representations (Charlesworth & Banaji, 2022b; Jackson et al., 2022). That is, language is a central

means for sharing representations between people (Beukeboom & Burgers, 2019), making it an ideal data source for capturing collective culture. Notably, language provides a means to share information not only

In summary, the current research combines (1) data from >200,000 human participants completing

positively/negatively these same attitude topics are represented in 9 contemporary corpora of text (e.g., newspapers, Internet text) as well as 200 years of historical book text, all trained using word embedding

models. These data equip us to address two guiding research questions, each elaborated below. First, to what extent do the latent patterns of our contemporary real-world language environments reflect our

collective attitudes? And, in particular, given proposed theoretical and empirical distinctions between implicit versus explicit attitudes (Cunningham et al., 2001; Greenwald & Banaji, 1995; Nosek & Smyth,

2007), do language environments relate more to implicit or explicit measures of attitudes? Second, as contemporary attitudes can be understood not only as products of our current moment but also of

persistent history, how far back (from 1800-2000) do we find traces of a relationship between contemporary attitudes and language representations?

Relationships of language to implicit versus explicit attitudes

NLP tools have quickly and widely been adopted as novel methods to study humans’ attitudes about social group and other concepts (Bhatia & Aka, 2022; Caliskan et al., 2016, 2022; Charlesworth et al.,

2021, 2022; Charlesworth & Banaji, 2019; Kozlowski et al., 2019; Lewis & Lupyan, 2020). Yet this work has been built from largely qualitative observations that language representations tend to contain the same

kinds of biases seen on attitude measures (e.g., language representations, like attitudes, contain an association of White=good/Black=bad; Caliskan et al., 2016). No quantitative evidence exists on the

strength of the relationship between statistics in language and human attitudes, let alone the moderators of the relationship (e.g., which types of attitudes, towards which attitude targets, and for how long in

history).

It remains unclear how evaluative representations in language will manifest in attitudes. On the one hand, to the extent that statistical structure in language shapes how concepts are associated in mind, we may find larger correlations between language and implicit measures, since implicit measures are proposed to reflect these latent associations and structures in our environment (Beukeboom & Burgers, 2019;

Charlesworth et al., 2022; Durkheim, 1924; Payne et al., 2017). Explicit measures of attitudes, by contrast, reflect how people choose to use that statistical information (Cunningham et al., 2007; van Bavel et al.,

separated from the latent statistical structure in language and show only weak relationships.

There is also a secondary methodological argument: language representations, like implicit measures, are indirect assessments of cultural patterns. As we describe in the Methods below, language representations are created by first taking co-occurrences of all words in large-scale text and representing

those co-occurrences as dense vectors of word meaning in distributed semantic space (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014). Relationships between these word vectors (the word embeddings) are then quantified to get out an index of, for example, how closely the cultural texts associate “goodness”/“Love” or “badness”/“Money” (Caliskan et al., 2016). As a result of this indirect measurement approach, some

authors assume that language representations must necessarily reveal the “implicit” biases of society (Bolukbasi et al., 2016; Caliskan et al., 2016; Manzini et al., 2019).

And yet, although the NLP methods may themselves be indirect, the underlying text data from the culture has characteristics that may make it more “explicit.” Text data are controlled and edited by authors and

may therefore be prone to social desirability or aspirational portrayals of society. Thus, when we study how groups, objects, or concepts are talked about in conversations or written about in books and newspapers, we may better capture a representation that reveals the explicit values and social norms of a society. The current work provides a direct quantitative test comparing the strength of relationships

between the latent representations of language and the attitudes revealed through implicit versus explicit measures. In so doing, we shed light on what kind of information language and attitudes are encoding from our environments.

Traces of contemporary attitudes in historical text

The latent patterns of language (such as those revealed through relationships among word embeddings) can provide insights into how society structures meaning (Berger & Packard, 2021; Bhatia & Aka, 2022) – how society links evaluative concepts like “good” and “bad” with the varied concepts of

human life ranging from “Religion” to “Love” to “Coffee.” The influence of history can be seen in how people filter the latent information through their values or goals and thus may dismiss or distort the information. For example, while “Religion”-“good” may be a persistent latent pattern of meaning in culture, people today may filter that information through contemporary values such as increasing

concerns about harms from the church (Pew Research Center, 2022). As such, it is possible that, even in the face of persistent latent meaning, different explicit values will be expressed across time.

When considering how language and attitudes relate to one another across time, a pattern of persistent

latent meaning alongside changing explicit values leads to predictions that language and implicit attitudes may be persistently related even when looking back at historical text from 200 years ago. This is because both implicit attitudes and language representations tap into similar latent regularities of meaning and cultural knowledge that will be resistant to change. Indeed, in related research, historical cultural patterns of slavery in the 1860s in the United States (Payne et al., 2019), have

By contrast, self-reported values and explicit attitudes are expected to change more (and, indeed, have

In the process of quantifying such empirical patterns, the current work contributes to a burgeoning theoretical understanding of how attitudes are reflections of language representations that quantify latent cultural

information both from this contemporary moment and stretching back across history.

## Methods

Open practices. All data and code are openly available through the project’s OSF page: https://osf.io/9kg5h/?view_only=10f7b39be5fa4cb0bdbb3cce7bbc2460. All analyses, data collection

and preparation procedures for contemporary analyses were formally preregistered at: https://osf.io/d63pt/?view_only=e3cc69e368cc40b4ad3830772d3859a6. Additional analyses with historical data were not preregistered.

Data sources.

Overview. To test questions of the relationship between contemporary attitudes and contemporary/historical language, we introduce a unique dataset bringing together: (1) humans’ implicit and explicit attitudes towards 55 diverse topics (about social groups, concrete objects and abstract

concepts); alongside (2) evaluative language representations of those same 55 topics, revealed in 9 diverse contemporary corpora and 200 years of historical book text, using 4 different methods to extract evaluative representations.

Pretrained word embeddings corpora. The growth of research in natural language processing and its application in the social sciences has provided many pretrained word embeddings – sets of word embeddings (defined below) that have already been trained using varied algorithms applied to massive corpora of naturalistic text, such Wikipedia, books, or large crawls of Internet text. To provide a robust test of the relationship between language representations and implicit and explicit attitudes, we first use 9

pretrained sets of contemporary embeddings, reflecting the largest and most commonly-used text sources in the computational and social sciences. Specifically, we use: (1) GloVe Common Crawl (with 840 billion word tokens); (2) GloVe Common Crawl (42 billion word tokens); (3) GloVe Wikipedia (6 billion word tokens); (4) GloVe Twitter (27 billion word tokens); (5) word2vec Google News (100 billion word

tokens); (6) word2vec Google Books (~ 500 billion word tokens, using only last decade from 1990–2000); (7) fastText Wikipedia, UMBC webbase corpus and statmt.org news (16 billion word tokens); (8) fastText

Extracting evaluative language representations.

Evaluative language representations (i.e., the positivity vs negativity in language) for 55 attitude topics were identified through word embedding associations. Details of how we (1) select the attitude topics, (2) choose stimuli to represent the topics, and (3) extract valence from language are elaborated in turn below.

Selecting attitude topics: Inclusion and exclusion criteria. We began with the list of 95 topics for which we had available implicit and explicit attitude data from the AIID dataset, and then determined which of these original 95 topics could be defensibly included in computing language representations. Because

most work examining evaluative representations in language has used pretrained static word embeddings (i.e., with each word having only one embedding that collapses across all word meanings), all embedding sets were also static embeddings. As such, we cannot accurately represent attitude topics

that require two-word stimuli (e.g., Bill Clinton) or have high polysemous meanings (e.g., coke, which refers to both the soda brand and the drug).

Three independent coders thus inspected the original list of 95 topics and the stimuli used for the IATs (i.e., the list of words used to represent the attitude topic in the original study). Each coder rated the topic as “include,” “exclude,” or “maybe include/exclude” based on whether that concept could be reasonably represented in language (e.g., did not include only two-word labels, did not include only polysemous or low-frequency terms). Looking at all ratings by all raters, we had moderate but significant agreement,  =

.44, z = 8.58, p < .001, with raters giving the same rating of inclusion/exclusion/maybe to approximately 50% of topics. When excluding those topics listed as “maybe” by at least one rater, the agreement on sure inclusion/exclusion was much higher, with  = .87, z = 4.79, p < .001, and the same rating of sure inclusion/exclusion to 82% of topics. All inconsistencies (i.e., any topic that received a “maybe” or different inclusion/exclusion from two raters) were discussed among raters and a final decision was made for inclusion.

Extracting valence from language. Evaluative language representations were operationalized using two methods to ensure robustness: (1) WEAT valence (computed from the Word Embeddings Association Test); and (2) MAC valence (computed using Mean Average Cosine similarity and valence ratings of top associated words). Each method was also computed using both longer and shorter word lists, resulting in four methods of extracting valence for each of the 55 topics.

WEAT valence. Valence from the Word Embeddings Association Test (WEAT) is computed by taking four lists of words, Group-A, Group-B, Positive, and Negative, and computing the relative average cosine

similarities between the Group word vectors and the Positive/Negative word vectors, and normalizing by the pooled standard deviation across all pairs of cosine similarities.

For example, to compute WEAT valence towards Straight (e.g., represented by words heterosexual, hetero, straight) versus Gay (e.g., homosexual, gay, lesbian), we would: (1) take the average of cosine similarities between the Straight words and all positive words, yielding the average Straight-positive association; (2) the average of cosine similarities between the Straight words and all negative words, yielding the average Straight-negative association; (3) the average of cosine similarities between the Gay words and all

positive words, yielding Gay-positive; and (4) the average of cosine similarities between the Gay words and all negative words, yielding Gay-negative. We would then take the difference between Straightpositive versus Straight-negative associations to yield a Straight-positive/negative association as well as the difference between Gay-positive versus Gay-negative associations to yield a Gay-positive/negative association. Next, we subtract the Gay-positive/negative from the Straight-positive/negative to yield the relative differences between the groups. Intuitively, the WEAT method, much like the Implicit Association

Notably, for every topic we also compute the WEAT in two ways. First, we calculate WEAT D scores by using the target group lists (as described above) and lists of the 100 most positive and 100 most

We term this WEAT D score as “WEAT D-long” since it uses the long list of valenced words to represent the positive/negative attributes. MAC valence. Valence from the Mean Average Cosine (Charlesworth et al., 2022; Manzini et al., 2019) is

computed by taking two lists of words, Group-A and Group-B, and then identifying the top-N words that have the highest relative cosine similarity to Group-A over Group-B. Next, each of the words in this top-N

list is replaced with its corresponding valence score from external ratings (provided by Warriner and

colleagues, 2014). We then take the average of the top-N words’ valence scores, resulting in an average valence score of Group-AvB on a 9-point scale ranging from − 4 (indicating all words would be very

negative) to + 4 (indicating all words would be very positive). This process is repeated for computing the average valence of Group-BvA. Finally, we take the difference between the average valence score for

Group-AvB and Group-BvA, resulting in a relative valence score more analogous to the WEAT and the IAT computations. Additionally, as for WEAT, we ensure robustness by computing the MAC scores in two

ways using both the top-10 words and top-50 identified words, which we term “MAC-short” and “MAClong,” respectively. For comparability to the WEAT D scores, we also z-score the MAC scores.

To make the MAC procedure more concrete, imagine that we are computing the MAC-top 10 valence for

Straight versus Gay. We would first find the top-10 words that have the highest cosine similarity to the Straight words and the lowest cosine similarity to the Gay words, resulting, example, in {conventional,

stable, unaffected, dependent, relaxed, straightforward, cordial, simple, consistent, casual}. Based on Warriner’s ratings, the average valence of these words is 0.94. We would then repeat the process for the

top-10 words with the highest cosine similarity to the Gay words and the lowest cosine similarity to the Straight words, resulting in {stupid, serious, worried, angry, kind, sexy, compulsive, curious, jealous,

greedy}, with an average valence of -0.47. Finally, we would take the difference between these two

average valence scores (0.94 – (-0.47)) to yield a relative MAC valence score of 1.41 that would then be zscored for comparability.

Extracting contemporary human attitudes.

Implicit attitudes. Implicit attitudes are represented as the average Implicit Association Test (IAT) D score

estimates for each of the 55 topics from the AIID dataset (Hussey et al., 2018). The IAT is a computerized


<!-- Page 13 -->


Page 13/27

reaction task in which participants are asked to make paired categorizations of group concepts (e.g.,

Straight, Gay) alongside attribute concepts (e.g., good, bad). The key contrast is performed between (a) “societally-congruent” blocks in which participants sort, for example, Straight + good to one key and Gay

+ bad to a second key, versus (b) “societally-incongruent” blocks in which participants sort, for example Gay + good to one key and Straight + bad to a second key. The difference in reaction time between these

blocks (divided by the pooled standard deviation of reaction times) gives the IAT D score, which is an estimate of the ease with which participants automatically associate group and evaluative concepts in

mind.

Explicit attitudes. Explicit attitudes are represented as the average relative preference estimates for each of the 55 topics, also drawn from the AIID dataset. Participants self-reported their attitude towards each

topic on a 7-point Likert scale from − 3 (e.g., strongly prefer Gay over Straight people) to + 3 (strongly prefer Straight over Gay people), with +/- 2 reflecting moderate preferences, +/- 1 reflecting slight

preferences, and 0 reflecting no explicit preferences.

strength (e.g., certainty, amount of thinking) and cultural pressures or prevalence of the attitudes.

Although not focal to the central question of this paper, we preregistered exploratory analyses to consider how 45 additional belief items of attitude strength and cultural beliefs may be moderators of the

Coding attitude domains. Finally, a secondary research question is how the domain of the attitude topic

(e.g., social group versus concrete object) may affect the relationship between language representations and implicit/explicit attitudes. To that end, the first and second authors inspected the list of 55 topics and

assigned them to one of three domains: social group (e.g., Straight-Gay), object (e.g., Cat-Dog), or abstract

Sample size and power for detecting effects. The final sample of contemporary language observations is

N = 1,980, derived from 55 topics with 36 extracted language representations per topic (4 valence extraction methods X 9 pretrained sets of embeddings); the final sample of historical language

observations is N = 4,400, derived from 55 topics with 80 extracted language representations per topic (4 extraction methods X 20 decades). While these sample sizes set upper limits on power to detect effects,

we offer two comments to address concerns around power.

First, all analyses are performed using Bayesian inference with pre-registered Regions Of Practical Equivalence or ROPE (Kruschke, 2018) and, as such, are less vulnerable to power-related concerns around

Type II errors from null hypothesis significance testing. Instead, the percentage of the model posteriors falling inside the ROPE can be used to directly quantify the amount of evidence in favor of a

hypothesized result (i.e., a meaningful relationship between language representations and attitudes) versus a null result (i.e., no relationship). Of note, for inference, we preregistered that, if > 95% of the

hypothesis (i.e., that language is related to attitudes); if > 95% of the posterior falls inside the ROPE, we have strong evidence in favor of the null. Any percentages below 95% that fall inside/outside the ROPE

Second, we reiterate that the majority of research to-date uses language representations as proxies for

## Results

Contemporary relationships between attitudes and language.

Turning first to relationships between contemporary attitudes and contemporary language, we organize results to answer: (1) How are the evaluative representations in distributed language (word embeddings)

related to aggregated implicit and explicit attitudes from humans? (2) How does the attitude domain (from relatively innocuous objects and abstract concepts to socially sensitive social groups) moderate

the link between language representations and humans’ implicit and explicit attitudes? After discussing

these preregistered primary analyses, we turn to preregistered exploratory analyses on (3) the relationships between language and additional beliefs (e.g., perceived cultural beliefs).

Contemporary relationships with implicit versus explicit attitudes. First, the Bayesian linear regression predicting (averaged) language valence from IAT D scores revealed strong evidence in favor of a

relationship between evaluative language representations and human implicit attitudes, Medposterior=

0.45, 95% Credible Interval (CIposterior) = [0.30, 0.61], with 100% of the posterior falling outside the region

of practical equivalence (ROPE). The slope value means that, for every 1 SD unit increase in the positivity of human implicit attitudes, the valence of contemporary language representations will increase by

approximately 0.45 SD (Fig. 1A), indicating a moderate effect size. When inspecting the 36 separate models (each measuring the relationship between implicit attitudes and an evaluative language

representation e.g., Glove:Common Crawl WEAT-long), results showed that > 95% of the posterior fell outside the ROPE for 32 out of 36 models (see Fig. 2 for the slope estimate across the 36 models). Such

results indicate that the relationship between implicit attitudes and evaluative language representations

is not only strong but robust across nearly every large-scale language dataset in use today.

In contrast, we found only weak evidence for a relationship between language representations and

human explicit attitudes, Medposterior= 0.15, CIposterior = [-0.05, 0.34], with only 68% of posterior falling

outside the ROPE, indicating more ambiguous evidence (Fig. 1B). Indeed, looking across all 36 models,

we found that only 2 out of the 36 models had > 95% of their posterior outside the ROPE (namely,

word2vec Books MAC-short and GloVe Wikipedia MAC-short; Fig. 2).

Finally, entering both implicit and explicit attitudes simultaneously (as preregistered), we found that the

relationship between language representations and implicit attitudes continued to be strong and

meaningful (with 100% of the posterior falling outside the ROPE), but the relationship with explicit attitudes weakened even further, such that only 26% of the posterior for explicit attitudes fell outside the

ROPE. Additionally, the interaction between implicit and explicit attitudes was not found to be a meaningful or positive predictor, Medposterior= 0.06, CIposterior = [-0.10, 0.21], 26% of posterior outside the

ROPE.

Moderation of contemporary relationships by domain of attitude topics. Beyond our focal question of the zero-order relationships between language representations and implicit/explicit attitudes, we also have a

unique opportunity to consider whether the relationships may be stronger for some kinds of attitudes than for others – namely contrasting attitudes for social groups, abstract concepts, or concrete objects.

Against our pre-registered hypotheses, we found no clear evidence for moderation by attitude domain.

First, we found no meaningful interactions between implicit attitudes and domain predicting evaluative language representations, whether between social groups vs. abstract concepts,

Medposterior(implicitXabstract) = 0.002, [-0.40, 0.41], 60% outside ROPE, or between social groups vs.

concrete objects, Medposterior(implicitXconcrete) = -0.39, [-0.86, 0.07], 91% outside ROPE (Fig. 3A). Thus,

evidence is most in line with the interpretation that implicit attitudes and language are linked regardless of attitude domain.

We also found no moderation of domain for explicit attitudes (Fig. 3B), with no meaningful interactions between social groups vs. abstract concepts, Medposterior(implicitXabstract) = 0.30, [-0.19, 0.80], 83%

outside ROPE, or between social groups vs. concrete objects, Medposterior(implicitXconcrete) = -0.01, [-0.56,

0.53], 70% outside ROPE. Conclusions persisted when the interaction between implicit attitudes-by-

domain and explicit attitudes-by-domain were entered simultaneously, as well as when a three-way interaction was entered (full details in SM).

However, visual inspection suggested a notable difference in the strength of implicit versus explicit attitudes specifically in the social groups domain. This led us to conduct a (non-preregistered) exploratory

model in which we compared the relationship of language to implicit vs. explicit attitudes for those 20

attitude topics that fell inside the social groups domain (Fig. 3A), as well as the other two domains separately. For social groups, results showed a meaningful interaction, Medposterior = -0.57, [-1.16, 0.02],

96% of posterior outside ROPE, such that the relationship between human attitudes and evaluative

language representations was stronger for implicit than for explicit attitude estimates in the social group domain. Interactions for concrete objects and abstract concepts did not pass thresholds for

meaningfulness, suggesting perhaps that abstract concept representations in language (Fig. 3C) are similarly captured by both implicit and explicit attitudes, while concrete objects (Fig. 3B) may not be

meaningfully captured by either.

The relationships between implicit attitudes and contemporary language have appeared robust and

magnitude of correlations across time, from essentially null r1800 = .06 to a small effect by 1990, r1990

language representations (weakly) overlap, they are overlapping because of shared endorsed values.

## Discussion

To what extent does language reflect our attitudes? For what type of attitudes (implicit or explicit) is the reflection strongest? And how has the reflection of attitudes in language distorted or persisted back

across historical time? To address these pressing theoretical and methodological questions, we

integrated two large-scale data sources: (1) data from participants completing tests of implicit and explicit attitudes (and additional explicit beliefs) about a diverse set of 55 attitude topics, including social

groups, concrete objects, and abstract concepts; alongside (2) data from 9 sets of contemporary texts and 200 years of historical book text, from which we extracted the evaluative language representations

(i.e., the positivity/negativity in language) towards the same 55 topics. Results revealed that language representations were strongly and robustly related to implicit, but not explicit, attitudes, and such strong

relationships of contemporary implicit attitudes and language were preserved even when looking back at texts from 200 years ago. Theoretically, the results shed new light on the implicit nature of large language

models as well as contribute to debates about how implicit social cognition reflects cultural patterns and

statistical regularities persisting across history. Moreover, methodologically, such findings provide firmer


<!-- Page 18 -->


Page 18/27

ground from which to build the growing area of computational social science (Lazer et al., 2009) and

encourage wide adoption of NLP methods for understanding patterns of implicit social cognition (even if less so for understanding explicit social cognition).

Robust evidence that evaluative language representations overlap with implicit attitudes.

Five converging pieces of evidence support the conclusion that evaluative language representations are

quantitatively and strongly aligned with human participants’ implicit attitudes across diverse topics. First,

contemporary language and contemporary implicit attitudes showed clear zero-order relationships, with an effect size that was moderate in magnitude, and 100% of the estimated posterior falling outside of a

pre-registered “region-of-practical-equivalence” (Kruschke, 2018). Second, these contemporary relationships were observed for 32 (out of 36) computed estimates of the evaluative language

representations, varying not only the underlying text corpus (e.g., Wikipedia versus Internet text versus books), but also the embedding algorithm (e.g., GloVe versus word2vec), and the method for extracting

valence (e.g., the Word Embeddings Association Test versus Mean Average Cosine-valence; Caliskan et

al., 2016; Charlesworth et al., 2022). Thus, impressively, evaluative language representations appear to reflect human implicit attitudes regardless of whether the text was more controlled (e.g., edited books) or

generally unedited and spontaneous (e.g., Twitter and Internet text).

Third, the relationship between implicit attitudes and evaluative language representations persisted

across three theoretically distinct domains of attitude targets – social groups, concrete objects, and abstract concepts – with similarly strong relationships across all domains. Though it is also noteworthy

that the distinction between implicit and explicit attitudes was largest for social groups where social desirability and personal values are most likely to play a role in divorcing explicit attitudes from statistical

regularities (Devine et al., 2002).

Fourth, the relationships between implicit attitudes and evaluative language representations persisted when controlling for explicit attitudes, with explicit attitudes showing no unique or additive relationship to

language representations (discussed further below). Perhaps even more notable: the relationship persisted after controlling for perceived cultural attitudes which, themselves, had a meaningful

relationship with language representations. Note that, if we had seen only the relationship between implicit attitudes and language, one might have argued that implicit attitudes (and language

representations) tap into a declarative, or explicit self-reported knowledge of what is in the culture.

However, the fact that implicit attitudes and language are linked above and beyond declarative cultural attitudes may imply that implicit attitudes tap into statistics distributed in sociolinguistic culture (e.g.,

Charlesworth & Banaji, 2021; Payne et al., 2017) that we may not be able explicitly self-report and easily perceive.

Fifth and finally, contemporary implicit attitudes collected from online participants in the 2000s were just as correlated with representations extracted from book text in the 1800s as they were with

representations extracted from Internet text today. This result lends new evidence to an emerging body of

work showing that historical patterns, such as slavery in the 1860s (Payne et al., 2019) or Jewish


<!-- Page 19 -->


Page 19/27

pogroms in the 14th century (Voigtländer & Voth, 2012), have long shadows that persist in contemporary prejudice. That implicit attitudes are more reflective of the past than are explicit attitudes (which had null

correlations with text from the 1800s) reinforces that implicit attitudes – and the statistical regularities they reflect – are vehicles to transmit culture across time.

Explicit attitudes are distinct from evaluative language representations.

In contrast to the strong link between language and implicit attitudes, there was a marked absence of a relationship between language and explicit attitudes. We found: (1) no meaningful zero-order relationship

between contemporary explicit attitudes and language; (2) for 34 of the 36 model specifications; (3) for three distinct domains of attitude topics; (4) even after including implicit attitudes or perceived cultural

attitudes; and (5) even for all 20 decades of text examined. In short, the absence of a relationship for explicit attitudes was just as robust as the presence of a relationship for implicit attitudes. Theoretically,

this finding suggests that explicit attitudes – even those explicit attitudes aggregated across large

samples of the population – capture endorsed, personal values (Charlesworth & Banaji, 2021) that are less direct reflections of statistics from shared, sociolinguistic environments. This counters the idea that

language representations may contain degrees of “explicit-ness” because they are derived from controlled, edited, and self-reported written texts.

Implications for using language to study social representations.

In addition to advancing theoretical understandings of attitudes and language, a secondary

methodological goal of the current research was to examine the latent but untested assumption that

evaluative language representations necessarily reflect human attitudes (an assumption that has underwritten the explosion of research using language to study attitudes; see Introduction). Having

comprehensively shown this to be true for humans’ implicit attitudes, we encourage the continued adoption of NLP in implicit social cognition research to expand across unprecedented timespans,

geographic locations, cultures, and demographics.

At the same time, we emphasize the continued care needed for interpretating what we measure in

language. For instance, many researchers may try to interpret language representations as indicative of

what the people of a given time period or location actually believed and personally endorsed. Such an interpretation is not supported from the current data. Yet, using language representations to examine

explicit attitudes does not appear to be defensible with contemporary data and methods of static word embedding models. Looking forward, we hope that continued developments in NLP might improve

researchers ability to quantify explicit attitudes from language. After all, explicit attitudes have many unique consequences for guiding behaviors and societal outcomes, sometimes above and beyond

implicit attitudes (e.g., Leitner et al., 2016; Riddle & Sinclair, 2019). If we want to use NLP to expand the scope of understanding psychologies and sociologies, it will be worthwhile to discover methods for

extracting multiple indicators of humans’ attitudes, both implicit and explicit.

# All human social groups are human, but some are more human than others: A comprehensive investigation of the implicit association of “Human” to US racial/ethnic groups

**Authors:** Kirsten N Morehouse; Keith Maddox; Mahzarin R Banaji

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Psychology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138 | bDepartment of Psychology, Tufts University, Medford, MA 02155

## Abstract

All humans belong to the species Homo sapiens. Yet, throughout history, humans have breathed life into the Orwellian adage that “All [humans] are equal, but some [humans] are more equal than others.” Here, participants staunchly rejected this adage, with the overwhelming majority of over 61,000 participants reporting that all humans are equally human. However, across 13 experiments, US White participants (and White participants abroad) showed robust evidence of an implicit Human=Own Group association. Conversely, Black, Latinx, and Asian participants in the United States did not demonstrate this bias. These results highlight the tendency among socially dominant groups to reserve the quality Human for their own kind, producing, even in the 21st century, the age-old error of pseudospeciation.

Keywords: implicit stereotypes, human–animal stereotypes, implicit association test, intergroup cognition, racial/ethnic stereotypes

## Abstract

All human groups are equally human, but are they automatically represented as such? Harnessing data from 61,377 participants across 13 experiments (six primary and seven supplemental), a sharp dissociation between implicit and explicit measures emerged. Despite explicitly affirming the equal humanity of all racial/ethnic groups, White participants consistently associated Human (relative to Animal) more with White than Black, Hispanic, and Asian groups on Implicit Association Tests (IATs; experiments 1–4). This effect emerged across diverse representations of Animal that varied in valence (pets, farm animals, wild animals, and vermin; experiments 1–2). Non-White participants showed no such Human=Own Group bias (e.g., Black participants on a White–Black/Human–Animal IAT). However, when the test included two outgroups (e.g., Asian participants on a White–Black/Human–Animal IAT), non-White participants displayed Human=White associations. The overall effect was largely invariant across demographic variations in age, religion, and education but did vary by political ideology and gender, with self-identified conservatives and men displaying stronger Human=White associations (experiment 3). Using a variance decomposition method, experiment 4 showed that the Human=White effect cannot be attributed to valence alone; the semantic meaning of Human and Animal accounted for a unique proportion of variance. Similarly, the effect persisted even when Human was contrasted with positive attributes (e.g., God, Gods, and Dessert; experiment 5a). Experiments 5a-b clarified the primacy of Human=White rather than Animal=Black associations. Together, these experiments document a factually erroneous but robust Human=Own Group implicit stereotype among US White participants (and globally), with suggestive evidence of its presence in other socially dominant groups.

By all relevant biological criteria (e.g., ability to interbreed and produce viable offspring; refs. 1 and 2), all humans—regardless of group membership—belong to a single species. And yet, history provides ample evidence of cultural pseudospeciation (3)—the tendency to treat culturally manufactured social groups (e.g., based on religion, language, ethnicity) akin to distinct biological species. These perceptions are psychologically potent and can drive intergroup differentiation. For example, Leyens et al. (4, 5) and Kteily et al. (6) demonstrated that this differentiation shapes perceived capacity for secondary emotions (e.g., pride and guilt) and judgments of a group’s evolutionary progress, respectively. Haslam (7) further suggested that groups can be differentiated based on their possession of traits central to “human” nature (e.g., imaginative and ambitious) or traits that distinguish humans from other animals (e.g., analytical and artistic).

As these examples illustrate, the field has not coalesced around a single definition of what it means to be more or less human (for a review, see ref. 8). However, data from these and related measures (e.g., mind attribution; ref. 9) converge to show that individuals tend to view three groups as more human: a) the self (e.g., refs. 10 and 11); b) ingroup members (e.g., refs. 12 and 13); and c) high-status groups (e.g., high-SES; ref. 14).

Related streams of research using more indirect methods (e.g., reverse correlation and fMRI; refs. 15–18) have similarly documented differences in affording the quality human to all human groups (for a review, see ref. 8). For instance, using a Go/No-Go association task (19), Saminaden et al. (20) observed a tendency to associate “Modern people” more with Human and “Traditional people” more with Animal; and using an Implicit Association Test (IAT; ref. 21), Bernard et al. (22) observed an implicit thin–human/obese–animal stereotype. The existence of such associations may be consequential, as Goff and colleagues (23) demonstrated; participants with stronger implicit associations between Black Americans (versus White Americans) with nonhuman primates also more strongly endorsed violence against Black suspects.

Taken together, research has demonstrated that the perceived humanity of social groups is not in line with biological or moral imperatives. Indeed, unlike judgments of preference, which are inherently subjective and equivocal, variability in the ascription of “human” to different social groups is a violation of a biological fact, making the existence of such stereotypes additionally noteworthy.

## Overview of the Present Report

Building upon this work, we conducted thirteen experiments (including seven supplemental experiments; SI Appendix, Appendix 2) to investigate the presence and strength of human–animal implicit stereotypes toward prominent racial/ethnic groups in the United States. Specifically, harnessing data from 61,377 participants (67% American residents), we aimed to a) establish whether racial/ethnic human–animal stereotypes can be detected on measures of implicit cognition and whether they diverge or align with explicit cognition; b) determine whether these stereotypes, if they exist, are robust across various contrasts (e.g., White–Black, White–Latinx, and White–Asian) and demographic subgroups (e.g., White and non-White groups); and c) explore the mechanisms underlying these stereotypes to clarify the meaning of the obtained results (e.g., clarifying the role of semantics, beyond evaluations).

Cultural pseudospeciation could theoretically occur across any socially manufactured category. We focused on race/ethnicity because individuals of European descent have been historically depicted as being more human (24–26). Further, race/ethnicity in the US context is sui generis given its multiethnic makeup, its relatively recent history of slavery, and explicit ascriptions of Black Americans as nonhuman (e.g., refs. 26–29). As such, participants’ stereotypes may refract these false beliefs or align with the fact that all racial/ethnic groups are equally human.

IATs were used to capture the strength of associations between pairs of racial/ethnic groups (e.g., White–Black) and the attributes Human and Animal. In most studies, a contrastive attribute of Animal was selected because a predominant way in which humans have opted to express the belief that outgroups are less human is to liken them to nonhuman categories of animal, and much of the experimental research to date has adopted it. Here, to ensure that the emergence of any group stereotype was not limited to specific representations of Animal, the attribute was represented within and across experiments by diverse representations of Animal (e.g., pets, farm animals, wild animals, and vermin) as well as generic terms like “beast” and “brute” (SI Appendix, Appendix 2). In yet other experiments, we compared Human to attributes besides Animal, including suprahuman (e.g., God, Gods) and other highly positive (e.g., Dessert, Flower) attributes.

Moreover, to determine the generality or specificity of these stereotypes, we examined whether human–animal stereotypes were confined to the White–Black contrast or reflected a more general tendency to associate certain groups (e.g., socially advantaged groups; ref. 14) with Human over Animal. Specifically, we measured human–animal stereotypes toward four prominent racial/ethnic groups that vary in their history and stereotype content within the US society: White, Black, Latinx, and Asian. In every test in the main text, White served as the comparison category. This provided the opportunity to explore whether implicit stereotypes emerge in all three contrasts (i.e., White–Black, White–Hispanic, and White–Asian) or only in particular contrasts (e.g., in the White–Black contrast but not White–Asian).

In addition to documenting the comparative strength of stereotypes across contrasts (e.g., White–Black versus White–Asian), the use of large samples allowed for subgroup analyses that are typically incomputable. Perhaps most importantly, we tested whether this Human=Own Group association was expressed by all participants or only by members of advantaged racial/ethnic groups (e.g., White Americans). Further, robust samples permitted tests of the role of other demographic characteristics, besides race/ethnicity, on human–animal stereotypes. For example, DeLuca-McLean and Castano (30) observed higher levels of infrahumanization (i.e., the denial of secondary emotions; ref. 5) among self-identified political conservatives, and Kteily et al. (6) observed a positive relationship between social dominance orientation (SDO) and the tendency to characterize non-White groups as less evolved. Such variation, if also observed on implicit measures, may reveal features that predict the emergence of implicit human–animal stereotypes. As such, potential variability across age, gender, political ideology, education, and religion was additionally assessed.

Finally, we explored two questions to probe the mechanisms underlying this effect. First, do implicit human–animal stereotypes measure anything beyond valence? That is, are “Human” and “Animal” merely proxies for “Good” and “Bad”, respectively, given the valence asymmetry of these terms? Or do any observed associations reflect genuine engagement with the semantic meaning of these terms? Directly testing these competing interpretations has important implications for the construct validity of the test. Second, which pole of the IAT drives human–animal stereotypes? The relative nature of the IAT makes it challenging to determine whether Human=White associations, Animal=non-White associations, or both drive these stereotypes. However, we created operationalizations designed to disentangle these possibilities. Ultimately, an individual’s racial or ethnic membership has no biologically defensible bearing on their degree of humanity. Accordingly, if an implicit stereotype tying Human more to one racial/ethnic group exists, then it is critical to document this deviation from accuracy, as denials of humanity have been associated with reduced altruism (31, 32) and empathy (33), increased aggression (34, 35), support for punitive policies (6), and greater acceptance of violence (23, 36).

## Experiments 1-2

As an initial point of departure, experiments 1-2 examined whether White and Black groups were equally and automatically associated with the attributes Human and Animal. These two groups were selected because of their unique position in US history and contemporary society. Black Americans have been depicted as less than human in media (e.g., refs. 26–29), and many were explicitly designated as such by the 1787 Three-Fifths compromise. Importantly, extending work by Goff et al. (37), the present experiments tested the association of White and Black with the more basic attributes Human and Animal.

Although a plenary representation of Human can be created with clear exemplars (e.g., man, woman, human, and person), nonhuman animals vary greatly across dimensions (e.g., valence and traits) that may influence the default mental representation of the term Animal. To represent multiple meanings of the term and therefore allow maximal generalization, four conceptualizations of Animal were created: pets, farm animals, wild animals, and vermin. On the one hand, associations between Animal and the social groups White and Black may vary according to the instantiation of Animal, suggesting that only specific representations of Animal discriminate between social groups. On the other hand, if all instantiations of the attribute Animal (e.g., pets and vermin) produce similar effects, then the conclusion that a core concept of Animal is involved can be more confidently drawn.

Moreover, given that the data were collected in the months following George Floyd’s murder, we administered an exploratory set of items about police violence and engagement in antiracism activities. These items are reported in SI Appendix, Appendix 3.

## Results and Discussion

### Explicit Attitudes.

On a 1 to 10 scale, participants reported feeling “somewhat” warm toward both White people (M = 6.95, SD = 2.10) and Black people (M = 7.56, SD = 1.95), with greater warmth reported toward Black than White people, t(846) = 8.93, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.31, 95% CI [0.24, 0.38]. This was true among both White participants (t(591) = 4.90, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.20, 95% CI [0.12, 0.28]) and non-White participants (t(240) = 8.16, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.53, 95% CI [0.39, 0.66]).*

### Explicit Stereotypes.

Participants clearly affirmed the humanity of both groups, associating Black (M = 1.63, SD = 1.15) and White (M = 1.78; SD = 1.29) targets with Human more than Animal.† In fact, less than 4% of participants reported that they considered either group to be more Animal than Human. Overall, the data suggest that, at least explicitly, participants affirmed the humanity of both groups.

### Implicit Stereotypes.

The critical result from experiments 1–2 is that implicit associations diverged both from biological fact and from participants’ self-reported beliefs. On all four IATs, Human was more associated with White, and Animal was more associated with Black (all IAT Ds > 0.17).

Despite considerable heterogeneity that was intentionally introduced to create diverse representations of the Animal attribute (e.g., varying in valence and trait attributions; ref. 38), one-sample t-tests indicated that this White–Human/Black–Animal (hereafter “Human=White”) association differed significantly from zero in all four animal conditions (all ps < 0.0001, all Cohen’s d > 0.40). The strength of association was statistically indistinguishable when the attribute Animal was represented by highly negative “vermin” or by more positive “pets,” t(22360) = 0.02, P = 0.988, Cohen’s d = 0.00, 95% CI [−0.04, 0.06]. In addition, a supplemental experiment (N = 2,912) demonstrated that this effect persisted when exemplars such as beast and brute served as the attribute stimuli (SI Appendix, Appendix 2, experiment S1). This evidence of a generalized association between Black with Animal (and White with Human) is not in conflict with Goff et al.’s (37) finding that Black Americans are relatively more associated with Apes and White Americans are relatively more associated with Big Cats. The same group can simultaneously be more associated with the high-level representation of Animal, relative to Human, and more associated with a specific class of animals (e.g., nonhuman primates), relative to another (e.g., big cats).

#### Effect of participant racial group on implicit stereotypes.

Participants’ self-reported race/ethnicity reliably predicted implicit human–animal stereotypes (see Table 1 for condition-specific means across experiments). As visualized in Fig. 1, White participants displayed an implicit Human=White association in all four animal conditions, IAT Davg = 0.22, t(7451) = 45.42, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.53, 95% CI [0.50, 0.55]. By contrast, Black participants did not display a symmetric Human=Black effect. Instead, and aligning with their self-reported beliefs, Black participants more equally associated Human and Animal with their own group and White, IAT Davg = –0.06, t(590) = –3.59, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = –0.15, 95% CI [–0.23, –0.07].

Interestingly, when the IAT captured stereotypes toward two outgroups (e.g., Asian participants taking a White–Black/Human–Animal IAT), participants (hereafter “third-party participants”) did not associate Human with both outgroups equally. Instead, third-party participants assigned the attribute Human more to the socially advantaged group (White) and Animal more to the socially disadvantaged group (Black) in every condition (Table 1). In fact, the Human=White association was only “slightly” stronger among White participants than among third-party participants, IAT Davg = 0.17, t(3021) = 22.2, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.41, 95% CI [0.37, 0.44].

Taken together, three results from experiments 1-2 are noteworthy. First, a sharp dissociation between explicit and implicit measures emerged. Despite overwhelming recognition of the humanity of Black and White social groups, White participants displayed a pervasive implicit Human=White association. Indeed, this factually inaccurate stereotype emerged when Animal was represented in multiple ways, from amiable pets to vermin. Second, only White participants displayed the Human=Own Group effect. Black participants’ associations more closely aligned with the biological and moral imperative that all racial/ethnic groups are equally human. Third and finally, third-party participants (e.g., Asian and Latinx participants taking a White–Black/Human–Animal IAT) demonstrated greater automatic ascription of humanity to White than to Black. This finding demonstrates the pervasive power of group status in shaping the minds of members of more and less advantaged groups alike.

## Experiment 3

Despite recognizing the humanity of both Black and White groups on self-report measures, White and third-party participants consistently displayed an implicit Human=White association (experiments 1–2). Are these results specific to the White–Black comparison? Or do they reflect a general tendency to ascribe Human more to White and Animal more to non-White groups? To test this, experiment 3 compared White not only to Black (providing a replication of experiments 1–2) but also to Latinx and Asian. These groups were selected because they are all prominent racial/ethnic groups in the United States but vary in their cultural histories and trait attributions. For instance, Black Americans are stereotyped as threatening, lazy, and poor (e.g., refs. 39 and 40). By contrast, Asian Americans are considered a model minority and are stereotyped as intelligent but shy (e.g., refs. 41 and 42). Thus, even if implicit human–animal stereotypes exist, they may emerge only in specific contrasts (e.g., White–Black). Further, to assess the extent to which this stereotype was widely shared, variability across six demographic characteristics—race/ethnicity, gender, political ideology, age, education, and religion—was newly examined.

## Results and Discussion

### Explicit Attitudes and Stereotypes.

#### Explicit attitudes.

Replicating experiment 1, participants reported feeling at least slightly warm (all means > 6) toward White, Black, Hispanic, and Asian groups. However, on the new measure of explicit preference, both White and non-White participants reported a relative preference for their own group, with group means ranging from 3.81 (White participants’ preference for White over Black) to 5.20 (Black participants’ preference for Black over White). Additional details are reported in SI Appendix, Appendix 3.

#### Explicit stereotypes.

Participants overwhelmingly affirmed the equal humanity of both groups. In fact, over 88% of non-White participants and over 96% of White participants endorsed the equal humanity of both groups.‡ In the minority (<7%) of cases where equal humanity was not affirmed, participants asserted a social correction by rating Black, Asian, and Hispanic groups as more human than White groups.

#### Implicit Stereotypes.

The primary aim of experiment 3 was to explore whether the implicit Human=White associations observed in experiments 1-2 were a) specific to the White–Black contrast or b) reflect a more general tendency to associate Human more with White and Animal more with non-White groups.

Replicating the results of experiments 1-2, White (IAT D = 0.27, t(4114) = 43.4, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.68, 95% CI [0.64, 0.71]) and third-party test takers (IAT D = 0.20, t(2563) = 26.0, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.51, 95% CI [0.47, 0. 55]) displayed an implicit Human=White association in the White–Black IAT condition, while Black participants displayed relative accuracy (IAT D = −0.02, t(500) = -2.23, P = 0.253, Cohen’s d = −0.05, 95% CI [−0.14, 0.04]).

Newly, and providing evidence of a general tendency to associate Human more with White, White participants displayed an implicit Human=White association in both the White–Hispanic contrast (IAT D = 0.33, t(3888) = 55.4, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.89, 95% CI [0.78, 1.03]) and the White–Asian contrast (IAT D = 0.32, t(3720) = 51.6, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.85, 95% CI [0.81, 0.88]). Similarly, third-party participants displayed an implicit Human=White association in both the White–Hispanic contrast (IAT D = 0.26, t(1903) = 30.4, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.70, 95% CI [0.65, 0.75]) and the White–Asian contrast (IAT D = 0.21, t(2563) = 27.8, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.55, 95% CI [0.52, 0.59]), but to a lesser degree than White participants (all ps < 0.005).

Interestingly, unlike Black participants, when their own group served as the contrast to White on the IAT (e.g., Asian participants taking a White–Asian/Human–Animal IAT), Latinx and Asian participants did not assign Human to both groups equally. Instead, Latinx participants (IAT D = 0.07, t(848) = 5.23, P < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.18, 95% CI [0.11, 0.25]) and Asian participants (IAT D = 0.04, t(325) = 2.02, P = 0.044, Cohen’s d = 0.11, 95% CI [0.003, 0.22]) displayed weak implicit Human=White associations. This pattern was replicated in the meta-analytic estimates (SI Appendix, Appendix 4). Overall, these results provide evidence for the robustness of the Human=White association across racial/ethnic comparisons and the disconnect between stated beliefs and implicit associations.

In SI Appendix, Appendixes 2 and 3, we probed the generality of human–animal stereotypes in two additional ways. First, we examined whether White participants’ Human=Own Group associations similarly emerged when Asian was represented as specific national/cultural (rather than racial/ethnic) entities. Providing evidence for the pervasiveness of human–animal stereotypes, White participants displayed implicit Human=Own Group associations when White was compared to groups identified as Chinese and Japanese (NS5 = 10,045; Cohen’s d > 0.82; SI Appendix, Appendix 2). Similarly, White Americans implicitly associated Human more with (White) Americans than (White) Canadians (NS6 = 875; Cohen’s d = 0.68; SI Appendix, Appendix 2); in fact, these Human=Own Group associations were just as strong as the effect in the White–Black contrast. These findings indicate that the results observed in experiments 1–3 were not specific to White versus non-White contrasts. Instead, they suggest a more general tendency for advantaged groups to associate their own group more with Human, regardless of whether the ingroup is demarcated by race, ethnicity, or nationality.

Second, we assessed whether this Human=White effect is unique to White Americans or emerges in White participants globally. Providing evidence for the generality of this stereotype across individuals who identify as White, non-US White participants consistently displayed Human=White associations, irrespective of country or geographic region of residence (SI Appendix, Appendix 3). Nevertheless, a related question remains: Is this Human=Own Group effect a signature of White participants, specifically, or of dominant groups in any society? We conducted a preliminary analysis of a dominant non-White group and find initial evidence that East Asians living in East Asia display an implicit Human=Own Group effect (In SI Appendix, Appendix 3). In other words, this effect may not be unique to White Americans or even White participants globally; instead, the effect may reflect the automatic association of Human to Own Group in any socially dominant group in a society, culture, or region. However, this test was an exploratory analysis that requires further confirmation in planned experiments.

Taken together, these data indicate that White participants display a pervasive, factually incorrect, implicit Human=Own Group stereotype. Moreover, they suggest that this stereotype a) extends beyond the White–Black comparison to other racial/ethnic and even national group comparisons and b) is not limited to Americans who identify as White. Indeed, this initial evidence suggests that a Human=White association emerges globally in those who identify as White.

#### Demographic moderators.

This consistency across target category contrasts is noteworthy, but is the effect similarly invariant across participant gender, age, level of education, political ideology, and religion? In other words, are these stereotypes observed across demographic subgroups or driven by particular demographic subgroups (e.g., older participants)?

Analyses revealed that education and religion did not moderate the strength of implicit Human=White associations in any of the three racial/ethnic contrasts (White–Black, White–Hispanic, White–Asian). Given the statistical power of these analyses, we can confidently assume that these null effects were not type II errors. Participant age was a significant predictor of stereotype strength only in certain contrasts.§ Specifically, in the White–Hispanic and White–Asian contrasts (but not in the White–Black contrast), older participants (>40 y old at the time of testing) displayed stronger implicit Human=White associations than younger participants (<20 y old at the time of testing). By contrast, gender and political ideology emerged as significant moderators of the effect,** with men and self-identified conservatives expressing slightly stronger implicit Human=White associations than women and self-identified liberals, respectively (Table 2).

## Experiment 4

Having demonstrated the robustness and generality of the Human=White effect, experiment 4 served to clarify the mechanisms underlying the effect. Specifically, experiment 4 examined whether implicit human–animal stereotypes capture anything beyond generalized valence or attitudes. That is, given the evaluative asymmetry of the attributes, with Human being more evaluatively positive in this context than Animal (NS7 = 491; Cohen’s d = 1.02; SI Appendix, Appendix 2), an association between Human and White may largely reflect valence consistency rather than a semantic association.

Past work has attempted to eliminate a valence confound by selecting attribute stimuli that have been equated for valence (43) or by demonstrating that these associations are not moderated by participants’ implicit preferences (37). Here, to provide a direct test of the latter, we implemented a valence decomposition technique introduced by Kurdi et al. (44). This technique requires each participant to complete two measures: an implicit stereotype IAT (e.g., White–Black/Human–Animal IAT) and an implicit attitude IAT (e.g., White–Black/Good–Bad IAT). Crucially, the analysis quantifies the variance left unexplained by a) implicit attitudes and b) measurement error. If the variance left unexplained is statistically distinguishable from zero, then the implicit Human=White stereotype effect can be said to be conceptually unique from an implicit attitude.

## Results and Discussion

Replicating the results of experiment 3, implicit Human=White associations were again observed in every race contrast (all IAT Ds > 0.18). Further, and in line with the well-established race attitude effect (e.g., refs. (45–47)), participants overall displayed an implicit preference for White, relative to Black (IAT D = 0.26), Hispanic (IAT D = 0.26), and Asian (IAT D = 0.20). Additionally, the correlations between implicit stereotypes (Human–Animal IATs) and implicit attitudes (Good–Bad IATs) were positive in all three racial/ethnic comparison: White–Black IAT (r = 0.43), White–Hispanic IAT (r = 0.31), and White–Asian IAT (r = 0.28). In fact, the correlations in the White–Black contrast approached the maximally expected correlations, given the IAT’s test–retest reliability of roughly r = 0.56 (48).

This initial result suggests that, as expected, implicit human–animal stereotypes detect an evaluative component, making a variance decomposition analysis necessary. In all cases, the 95% bootstrap confidence interval for residual true variance (RTV) did not include zero (see Table 3 for the full variance decomposition output). These data suggest that implicit Human=White associations are not fully reducible to valence alone. Instead, the Human–Animal IATs do detect a semantic association between Human with White (and Animal with non-White), independently of valence.
